newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: MARCO POLO NEEDS TO REPLENISH LANDBANK.
newsitem.headline: MARCO POLO NEEDS TO REPLENISH LANDBANK.

text.p: Marco Polo Developments Ltd needs to step up its efforts to replenish its landbank to convince investors of a transformation into a quality property developer, investment analysts said on Tuesday.
Marco Polo, 74-percent owned by Hong Kong's Wheelock & Company, said on Monday it would redevelop its Marco Polo Singapore hotel site into a condominium project in 1999.
Analysts said the long awaited announcement from the hotel company came as no surprise as the hotel had underperformed in recent years.
The proposed property project is expected to reap sales of Singapore $760 million for the group.
"The news is not unexpected. The hotel has not been able to compete and its GOP (gross operating margins) have been below market rates," said Kerryn Tay, investment analyst with GK Goh Securities.
Tay said he expected the condominium project to bring in pre-tax profits of about S$500 million for the group starting from financial year 1999/2000.

But after the hotel site is turned into condominiums, the group has no more land for development. Its property portfolio comprises a commercial complex in Orchard Road, Wheelock Place, and the Ardmore Park condominium project under construction.
"The current perception of the company is that it is just a three asset company," said Lim Chung Chun, investment analyst with ING Baring Securities.

Lim said the company will have a lot of cash pouring in from its Ardmore Park project, about S$1 billion in pretax profit, and from the hotel redevelopment, which he expected to bring in S$380 million in pretax profit.
"The cash flow is going to be very strong but they have not acquired anythying," he said.
Analysts said the company has been participating in recent private and public land sales but so far seems to be unsuccessful in getting any sites.

"They could be a bit too conservative in their bidding. And their share price is going to languish around current levels until people can see they have made a real effort to replenish their landbank," said Tay.
Marco Polo's share price has been trading between the S$2.95 to S$3.20 band, about 20-25 percent below its net tangible asset of about S$3.80 a share.
"The share price is not going to perform until they can get a stake in a good property project to show they can sustain their earnings stream," Tay said.
However, Lim said Marco Polo should not be criticised for failing to acquire sites at high prices.
"There will be more acquisition opportunities going forward into the next 12-24 months," he said.
